title: Sovereign citizens exposed: Uncovering a multimillion-dollar tax scam | the fifth estate
summary: CBC Fifth Estate investigation into Canadians who used sovereign-citizen trust theories to obtain multimillion-dollar tax refunds, the paid courses behind them, and sovereign violence abroad.

assertions.quote: And that is not a thing. We do not have a trust assigned to you.

verdicts.note: Birth certificates are vital-statistics records, not securities; tax agencies and courts confirm no such accounts exist.
The court finds the claim of a Treasury trust account funded from a birth certificate 'patently frivolous'; it 'strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund ... actually exists'.
Treasury says a birth certificate has no monetary value, cannot be used for purchases or to claim bonds, and the 'Exemption Account' is fictitious and does not exist in the Treasury system.
Gold Shield Alliance promised to zero debts via A4V payments from a Treasury 'birth trust account'; the scheme was described and rebutted in Alberta Treasury Branches v Nielson.

The redemption theory that a birth certificate is an asset worth up to $2 million cleared through the Treasury is described by courts as clearly nonsense, and the Treasury keeps no accounts individuals can draw on.
The birth-certificate 'Birth Bond' is presented as part of a false shadow history built on the strawman, which the author calls a myth with no legal basis.

assertions.quote: Did they teach you the right things or did they just teach you how to properly commit fraud?

verdicts.note: Tax agencies treat these refunds as obtained by fraud, freeze accounts and garnish wages; criminal charges vary.

Trust 'untaxing' and SSN-card trust filings are frivolous and draw civil and criminal penalties (Lizalek: trust held nonexistent, income taxed, penalties); the document does not show refunds actually paid and later recovered.

assertions.quote: It doesn't mean that what he believes in is working. It just means that they have, you know, figured out how to manipulate CRA systems.

verdicts.note: Documented CRA and IRS cases show bogus returns paid out because withholding claims were not checked before refunds were issued.
The Fiscal Arbitrators scam triggered undeserved tax refunds by claiming fictional business expenses with the strawman, later litigated in the Tax Court.
Treasury: some sites sell videos, webinars and coaching on birth-certificate bonds; 'the scammers intend to profit from this story by selling their bogus wares'.
Gurus market pseudolaw for profit: Menard's ACCP sold $250 'debit cards' after $200 membership fees and the card never materialized; other gurus sell information packages for $250 to $3,000.
Promoters sold untaxing packages, books and seminars (Meredith's businesses; a corporation-sole program sold to over 300 people), the same products the claim describes in the tax-protester setting.

Gurus are described as conmen who sell OPCA concepts for a price via seminars, books and DVDs; examples include Porisky taking about 7 percent of 800 students' income and a $500 plus 2 x $5,000 status scheme.
Websites and some lawyers charge thousands of dollars for pseudolaw advice on fines, mortgages and rates; some clients lose their homes.
The authors call OPCA litigants victims of conman gurus who sell supposed secrets of the concealed law; trial decisions report template documents sold as commercial products.
FBI describes sovereign citizens charging fees for seminars on redemption schemes, selling CDs/DVDs and fake documents, and charging for 'consultant services' to prepare paperwork.
Review describes gurus selling seminars and workshops promising debt relief and emancipation, paid bond-process services for prisoners, and paid online 'sovereign rights' subscriptions.

assertions.quote: police stops involving sovereigns sometimes turn deadly, with officers killed.

verdicts.note: The review cites the FBI and a criminologist's count of at least 250 violent cases, but it calls adherents only 'occasionally' violent and gives no police-specific rate.
FBI reports lone-offender sovereign-citizen extremists killed six law enforcement officers from 2000 to 2011 and that challenges at traffic stops can quickly escalate to violence.
In a 2013-14 survey of state and local intelligence officers, 86% agreed sovereign citizens were a serious terrorist threat, ranking them first; this measures perceived threat, not actual violence.
Open-source compilation found 75 instances of harm or attempted harm to police, 27 officers killed (1983-July 2020) and 65 wounded; media-based and possibly incomplete.

Systematic review: violent crimes are mainly directed at police and state agents; DHS found officers were victims in 20 of 24 violent sovereign incidents 2010-2014, though the violence is mostly reactive.

assertions.quote: Years later, the pandemic helped spread sovereign ideas.

verdicts.note: The review cites sociologist Stephen Kent linking surges of interest in pseudolaw to periods of social and economic distress; a secondhand citation, not its own data.
The review links growth to hardship (US 1980s farm debt crisis; Irish foreclosures after 2008) but does not test whether hardship is the main driver.
US sovereign-citizen influence intensified during the 2020-21 Covid restrictions; earlier the Posse Comitatus drew farmers facing foreclosure in the 1970s-80s.
FBI predicted growth fuelled by the Internet, the economic downturn and seminars; a forecast, not a measured comparison of spread across periods.

In a German press sample, 68% of those with known motives had financial difficulties and 45% work problems such as insolvency, and sovereigns used Covid to mobilize; this is individual hardship, not a measured surge during crises.

assertions.quote: At the core, it's a transnational phenomenon with the same ideological base.

verdicts.note: An Australian driver argued he was a 'citizen sovereign' to whom Queensland laws did not apply, with strawman-like 'BRADLEY person' language: one instance of US-style arguments abroad.

Review traces most modern pseudolaw to the US Sovereign Citizen movement, transmitted from about 2000 to Canadian Detaxers and Freemen, then to the UK, Commonwealth, the German Reichsbuerger and other European groups, adapted to each system.

A Canadian court counsel's history traces US sovereign-citizen ideas (strawman, A4V, UCC) imported into Canada and Canadian Freeman concepts exported to Australia, the UK, Ireland, Jersey, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Norway, though some gurus did little local adaptation.
A survey of 200+ Australian and NZ cases finds US sovereign-citizen pseudolaw migrated there from about 2010 and adapted to local legal discourse; US gurus ran speaking tours there in the 2010s.
Populations in a dozen or more countries have adopted the US-derived Pseudolaw Memeplex; Canadian Detaxers and Freemen adapted it around 2000.
Review documents the movement in Canada, the UK, Ireland, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia, Russia ('USSR citizens') and Germany (Reichsbuerger), with local variants of the same tactics.
Review finds Canadian and German sovereigns take cues from US developments while adapting narratives to local law and history (e.g. Third Reich law in Germany, common law in Canada).

assertions.quote: They won. They had a success, right? They were validated in their belief systems.

verdicts.note: Researchers of conspiracy belief describe intermittent apparent successes as strongly reinforcing, though measured evidence is mostly qualitative.
Menard held up an unrelated NZ jury acquittal as proof Freeman theories work, and Clifford read reported losses as evidence of hidden wins; anecdotal.
A Freeman guru's status 'escalated dramatically' after he claimed Freeman techniques got him released (charges were stayed after a month in remand).
